list.listitem: Persistent proteinuria is a significant predictor of progressive renal disease and cardiovascular disease. B

Annual screening may be considered for adults at high risk of kidney disease (eg, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, HIV) as it is somewhat cost effective (ie, $18,000/quality-adjusted life year [QALY] for hypertensive adults). C
In type 1 diabetic patients with duration ≥5 years or type 2 patients at diagnosis, a urine microalbumin should be tested annually regardless of spot urinanalysis results. B
Urine microalbumin is used for screening diabetics while a routine urinalysis is used for other groups. C
Although 24 hour urine collection for protein and creatinine are considered the gold standard, a spot urine to creatinine ratio can be used to estimate quantity of proteinuria. C

background.definition: Proteinuria is a non-specific term that describes any situation when a greater than normal amount of protein is excreted into the urine. Traditionally it is defined as >150 mg protein excreted over 24 hours. Excretion of albumin in the urine is called (micro)albuminuria. Although the 2 terms are not synonymous, they are often used interchangeably.

list.listitem: Proteinuria is an early and significant predictor of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) progression (RR 5.56; 95% CI).
It is also a significant marker of cardiovascular risk in both diabetic and non-diabetic subjects.
Diabetic glomerulosclerosis (most common).
Hypertensive renal parenchymal disease.
Minimal change disease (most common in children).
Infectious (ie, post-strep glomerulonephritis, HIV).
IgA glomerulonephritis.
Transient (benign) causes include: fever and acute illness, dehydration, heavy exercise, emotional stress, and UTI.
Orthostatic or postural hypotension are a benign cause of persistent proteinuria.

Pathophysiological causes are glomerular, tubular, and overflow: Glomerular: increased glomerular capillary permeability to protein. Tubular: decreased tubular reabsorption of proteins in glomerular filtrate. Overflow: increased production of low-molecular weight proteins.
The USPSTF concluded that the evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of routine screening for chronic kidney disease in asymptomatic adults.
The American College of Physicians recommends against screening for CKD in asymptomatic adults without risk factors.
Screening urinanalysis in asymptomatic children or adults under age 60 is not beneficial or cost effective.
At age 60, screening by urine dipstick every 10 years may be cost effective ($53,000/QALY in one study).

Screening in adults at high risk (eg, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, HIV) is more cost effective (ie, $18,000/QALY for hypertensive adults) and should be considered.
Screening by urine dipstick in pregnancy is a poor predictor for preeclampsia with positive predictive values between 2% and 11%.
Lifestyle modifications including exercise and diet aimed at reducing obesity, reducing blood pressure, preventing or treating diabetes, and preventing or treating hyperlipidemia.
Avoid tobacco use.
Minimize non-steroidal anti-inflammatory use (excluding aspirin).
Diet modification including moderate protein restriction (.60-.75 g/kg daily) and low salt (4-6 g sodium chloride/day).
Blood pressure control: if proteinuria <1 g/24 hr, then target is <130-135/80-85 mmHg; if proteinuria >1 g/24 hr, then target is <125/75 mmHg.
First line antihypertensive: ace inhibitor.
Second line: angiotensin receptor blocker or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker.
Third line: beta or alpha blocker, dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker.
Blood glucose control: target is HgA1C <7%-8%.
Lipid management: LDL cholesterol <100 mg/dL. Statins may reduce kidney function loss in patients with coronary artery disease.
Discontinue cigarette smoking.
There are additional recomendations to limit complications after diagnosis of chronic kidney disease (CKD) including managing anemia, hyperparathyroidism, malnutrition, and congestive heart failure.
Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors are recommended for adults with CKD and high risk of CKD progression and complications, regardless of type 2 diabetes status.
Annual urinalysis is indicated for diagnosing proteinuria in hypertensive patients. C
There is insufficient evidence to recommend screening for proteinuria in asymptomatic patients.B
In adults proteinuria is defined as >300 mg/day on 24 hour urine collection, >30 mg/dL on spot urine dipstick, or >200 mg/g on spot urine protein to creatinine ratio.
Urine albumin to creatinine ratio is the preferred measure; microalbuminuria is defined as >30 mg urine albumin/gram creatinine.
There are some recommendations that the value should be adjusted based on race and sex.
In children ranges can vary significantly depending on age. Using 24 hour urine collection: >100 mg/m2/24 h. Using UPr/Cr: >.2 mg/mg in children ≥2 years and >.5 mg/mg in children 6 to 24 mo of age.
Typically patients presenting with proteinuria will be asymptomatic. History and physical should be directed at identifying potential underlying cause of the proteinuria.

History can identify potential causes of transient proteinuria: recent increase in dietary protein, heavy exercise, recent febrile illnesses, urinary symptoms suggestive of infection, or extreme emotional stress.
Blood pressure should be obtained.
If nephrotic syndrome is suspected, physical exam should include evaluation for edema, especially of eyes, feet, and hands.
There are several methods for assessing proteinuria.

24 hour urine collection (gold standard): most accurate way of quantifying proteinuria, also allows you to quantify dietary sodium, potassium, protein, and creatinine clearances. A major disadvantage is that it is inconvenient for the patient.

A meta-analysis of 16 studies of point-of-care (POC) tests for proteinuria found that the quantitative test, but not the semi-quantitative test, had high enough sensitivity to rule out proteinuria from a single urine sample.

Spot urinanalysis: easiest and most cost-effective method of screening, indicated for assessing cardiovascular risk in hypertensives and routine screening. Can be false positive if urine is alkaline (ph >8.0) or if urine is very concentrated (specific gravity ≥1.025).

Spot urine protein to creatinine ratio: the simplest to quantify proteinuria, it is not as accurate as 24 hour urine collection. This is the preferred method for quantifying proteinuria in children because of difficulty obtaining timed urine collections.
Spot albumin/creatinine ratio for microalbuminuria: indicated for assessing risk of glomerulopathy in diabetics.
Patients with proteinuria should also have urine microscopy performed (see for interpretation).

A number of evolving biomarkers are being investigated for use in predicting which patients with chronic kidney disease are at highest risk or progression to failure, but none are currently recommended.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to evaluation of the patient with proteinuria.
